newsitem.title: FRANCE: More French films got subsidies in 1996 - CNC.
newsitem.headline: More French films got subsidies in 1996 - CNC.

text.p: More French films received a state subsidy in 1996 than in 1995, but the money value of the subsidies was slightly down overall, according to the Centre National du Cinema's (CNC) report for the year.

The CNC, a state body which aims to counteract the box office domination of American films in France, funded 104 films in 1996 for a total subsidy of 2.53 billion francs, compared with 97 films in 1995 for a total of 2.72 billion francs.
The year proved to be a good one for the French film industry and "nothing makes us think that this trend would not continue", Marc Tessier, CNC managing director, told a news conference on Thursday.
The industry's annual turnover is some four billion francs, including box office takings, television and video receipts.

In addition to the CNC subsidies, pay television channel Canal Plus in 1996 pre-purchased 85 films initiated by the French film industry for a total of 605.4 million francs and spent 73 million francs on 27 films co-produced by French and foreign film makers.

Canal Plus, for which cinema is a specialist area of coverage, contributed 27 percent of the private funding for French films in 1996, including co-productions with foreigners, up from 25.5 percent in 1995.

Terrestrial television channels pre-purchased 65 films in the year, of which 56 had also received a CNC subsidy, for a total investment of 486.6 million francs, a rise of eight percent over their 1995 investment.
Of this, TF1 put up 221.2 million francs, public channels France 2 and France 3 spent 120.9 million and 99 million respectively, while La Sept paid out 28.5 million and M6 15 million.
The terrestrial channels together contributed 19.1 percent of the total funding received by the French film industry in 1996, up from 16.8 percent in 1995.
"Overall, 46 percent of French films were produced by television, or around one film in two", Tessier said.
He said that French cinema was growing at three to four per cent a year in value, while television's growth was between seven and eight per cent.

The Conseil Superieur de l'Audiovisuel (CSA), the French broadcasting regulator, is planning to make digital, cable and satellite channels comply with the same obligations to carry a fixed percentage of French films as terrestrial channels must currently observe, he added.
This should benefit the French film industry, he said.

The French mutual funds which specialise in investing in film production invested in 39 films in 1996 against 38 in 1995, but the global amount invested fell sharply to 128.55 million francs from 153.65 million in 1995.
Of these, Sofinergie spent 37.2 million francs on 18 films et Cofimage 32 million on 14 films.
